## [1] 1000
set.seed(1023)

##  int [1:900] 982 194 799 315 6 899 186 300 640 555 ...

prop.table(table(credit2$default))
## 
##        No       Yes 
## 0.6966667 0.3033333
#Entropy = -SUM(pi*log_2(pi)) where pi is the proportion of each class in the response variable (Default).


# using function to calculate entropy and then subtracting weighted entropy from total enetropy to get information gain.


set.seed(1023)

# Step 1: Load necessary library
library(dplyr)


# Step 2: Load necessary functions

# Function to calculate entropy
calc_entropy <- function(probabilities) {
  -sum(probabilities * log2(probabilities),na.rm = TRUE)
}

# Calculate entropy for the target variable "default"
target_entropy <- {
  probs <- prop.table(table(credit2$default))
  calc_entropy(probs)
}
print(paste("Total Entropy for Default:", round(target_entropy, 3)))
## [1] "Total Entropy for Default: 0.885"
# Step 3: Calculate entropy for each split
# Define a function to calculate weighted entropy for a split
calc_weighted_entropy <- function(credit2, feature, target) {
  feature_levels <- unique(credit2[[feature]])
  
  weighted_entropy <- 0
  
  for (level in feature_levels) {
    subset_data <- credit2[credit2[[feature]] == level, ]
    target_probs <- prop.table(table(subset_data[[target]]))
    level_entropy <- calc_entropy(target_probs)
    weight <- nrow(subset_data) / nrow(credit)
    weighted_entropy <- weighted_entropy + weight * level_entropy
  }
  
  return(weighted_entropy)
}

# Calculate weighted entropy and information gain for each feature
weighted_entropy_checking <- calc_weighted_entropy(credit2, "checking_balance", "default")
weighted_months_loan_duration <- calc_weighted_entropy(credit2, "months_loan_duration", "default")
weighted_entropy_credit_history <- calc_weighted_entropy(credit2, "credit_history", "default")
weighted_entropy_purpose <- calc_weighted_entropy(credit2, "purpose", "default")
weighted_savings_balance <- calc_weighted_entropy(credit2, "savings_balance", "default")
weighted_entropy_employment_length <- calc_weighted_entropy(credit2, "employment_length", "default")
weighted_entropy_residence_history <- calc_weighted_entropy(credit2, "residence_history", "default")
weighted_entropy_property <- calc_weighted_entropy(credit2, "property", "default")
weighted_entropy_housing <- calc_weighted_entropy(credit2, "housing", "default")
weighted_entropy_existing_credits <- calc_weighted_entropy(credit2, "existing_credits", "default")


#calculate the information gain.


# Step 3: Calculate Information Gain for each feature

# Calculate Information Gain
info_gain_checking <- target_entropy - weighted_entropy_checking
info_gain_duration <- target_entropy - weighted_months_loan_duration
info_gain_credit_history <- target_entropy - weighted_entropy_credit_history
info_gain_purpose <- target_entropy - weighted_entropy_purpose
info_gain_savings_balance <- target_entropy - weighted_savings_balance
info_gain_employment_length <- target_entropy - weighted_entropy_employment_length
info_gain_residence_history <- target_entropy - weighted_entropy_residence_history
info_gain_property <- target_entropy - weighted_entropy_property
info_gain_housing <- target_entropy - weighted_entropy_housing
info_gain_existing_credits <- target_entropy - weighted_entropy_existing_credits



# Print the results
print(paste("Information Gain for checking balance:", round(info_gain_checking, 3)))
## [1] "Information Gain for checking balance: 0.177"
print(paste("Information Gain for loan duration:", round(info_gain_duration, 3)))
## [1] "Information Gain for loan duration: 0.123"
print(paste("Information Gain for credit history:", round(info_gain_credit_history, 3)))
## [1] "Information Gain for credit history: 0.133"
print(paste("Information Gain for purpose:", round(info_gain_purpose, 3)))
## [1] "Information Gain for purpose: 0.11"
print(paste("Information Gain for savings balance:", round(info_gain_savings_balance, 3)))
## [1] "Information Gain for savings balance: 0.113"
print(paste("Information Gain for employment length:", round(info_gain_employment_length, 3)))
## [1] "Information Gain for employment length: 0.098"
print(paste("Information Gain for residence history:", round(info_gain_residence_history, 3)))
## [1] "Information Gain for residence history: 0.09"
print(paste("Information Gain for property:", round(info_gain_property, 3)))
## [1] "Information Gain for property: 0.104"
print(paste("Information Gain for housing:", round(info_gain_housing, 3)))
## [1] "Information Gain for housing: 0.1"
print(paste("Information Gain for existing credits:", round(info_gain_existing_credits, 3)))
## [1] "Information Gain for existing credits: 0.089"
# Choose the best features based on information gain

information_gains <- c(
  checking_balance = info_gain_checking,
  months_loan_duration = info_gain_duration,
  credit_history = info_gain_credit_history,
  purpose = info_gain_purpose,
  savings_balance = info_gain_savings_balance,
  employment_length = info_gain_employment_length,
  residence_history = info_gain_residence_history,
  property = info_gain_property,
  housing = info_gain_housing,
  existing_credits = info_gain_existing_credits
)

sorted_information_gains <- sort(information_gains, decreasing = TRUE)

print("variables sorted by Information Gain in decsending order:")
## [1] "variables sorted by Information Gain in decsending order:"
print(round(sorted_information_gains, 3))
##     checking_balance       credit_history months_loan_duration 
##                0.177                0.133                0.123 
##      savings_balance              purpose             property 
##                0.113                0.110                0.104 
##              housing    employment_length    residence_history 
##                0.100                0.098                0.090 
##     existing_credits 
##                0.089
# the vaiable with max info gain would be the best split 
# the checking history is the best split followed by credit history and months loan duration. the least best split is existing credits.

CONCLUSION:The variable with max info gain would be the best split. The checking history is the best split followed by credit history and months loan duration and the least best split is existing credits.

# response = diabetes test result--test
# pred = pregnant ,glucose,diastolic,triceps  ,insulin  ,bmi, diabetes , age,
# total data obsrvtn = 768

set.seed(456) 

#split the data into two parts 70-30 split
DataSplit<-createDataPartition(y = pima1$test, p = 0.7, list = FALSE)

#creating the train and test data set

p_tr <- pima1[DataSplit,]   #training data
p_tes <- pima1[-DataSplit,]  # test data


p_tr$test <- as.factor(p_tr$test)

library(tree)



# tree model

# training data 

tree_diabetes <- tree(test ~ ., data = p_tr)

summary(tree_diabetes)

## tree(formula = test ~ ., data = p_tr)

plot(tree_diabetes)
text(tree_diabetes, pretty = 0)

# Assessing if  cross validation and pruning will improve the model

cv_tree_diabetes  <- cv.tree(tree_diabetes, FUN = prune.misclass)

plot(cv_tree_diabetes$k, cv_tree_diabetes$dev, type = "b", xlab = "Cost Complexity Parameter (k)", ylab = "Deviance")

# checking the lowest deviance and the corresponding size to assess the best model.

# lowest deviance is 60 and size is 4

pruned_tree_diabetes <- prune.misclass(tree_diabetes, best = 4)

Evaluation of the model on test data:

Accuracy: This model tree has an accuracy of 81.2 percent which means it is a good model. Precision: The precision of 77.14 perecnt is also good as it can correctly predict 77 percent positive cases. Recall : Of the all positive cases it did identify 65.85 percent correctly or true positives . This is moderate performance as it identified only 27 true positives and the 8 were false positives.

Overall the model is good i terms of accuracy with 81.2 percent accuracy but has limited ability in terms of predicting true positives. So we may need to improve overall precision by boosting.

b-) Use Bagging method on the train data set and evaluate the performance on the test data set. (5 pts)

Step 1: use p_tr for bagging method.

Step 2: use ipred library for bagging model creation.

Step 3: Analyse performance on test data by means of predict fn and confusion matrix - accuracy, precision , recall and f1 score with true and false positives .

# p_tr

p_tr$test <- as.factor(p_tr$test)
p_tes$test <- as.factor(p_tes$test)

library(ipred)

set.seed(456) 

pima_bag <- bagging(test ~ ., data = p_tr, nbagg = 25)
summary(pima_bag)

  1. accuracy - Overall accuracy is 80.34 percent which is good
  2. precision - total positives is 76.47 percent which is good however only 63.4 percent are true positives. 3.recall - it predicts 63.41 percent of true positives which is moderate.

c-) Use Boosting method on the train data set and evaluate the performance on the test data set. (5 pts)

Step 1: change the response into factors .

Step 2: use library C50 for boosting with 10 trials .

Step3: analyse the model on train data

Step 4: evaluate the performance on tests data using cross table and confusion matrix

Step 5:

# boosting 

library(C50)

p_tr$test <- as.factor(p_tr$test)
p_tes$test <- as.factor(p_tes$test)


# Train the boosting model on the training data with 10 trials
pima_boost10 <- C5.0(test ~ ., data = p_tr, trials = 10)

# Summarize the boosting model
summary(pima_boost10)

bagging_accuracy <- confusion_matrix_p$overall['Accuracy']

bagging_recall <- confusion_matrix_p$byClass['Recall']
bagging_f1 <- confusion_matrix_p$byClass['F1']

bagging_metrics <- c(Accuracy = bagging_accuracy,Precision = bagging_precision, Recall= bagging_recall ,F1 = bagging_f1)



boosting_accuracy <- confusion_matrix_boost$overall['Accuracy']

boosting_f1 <- confusion_matrix_boost$byClass['F1']

Precision- Boosting again has a good precision percentage of 82 perecnt better than the other models. 3. recall - Boosting has the highest recall value and is hence good at predicting true positives compared to others. The tree model is the next better model and Random forest model is the worst at predicting true positives or recall. 4. F1 score - boosting has the best F1 score of 76 compared to other models.

Boosting model is based on the trial and error and boosts or improving the performance based on the errors found in the earlier trial. This finding makes sense.

Overall, i would choose the boosting model among these based on the performances on the test data with good accuracy and precision and recall.

Problem 3

Refer to the Prostate cancer data set. Serum prostate-specific antigen (PSA) was determined in 97 men with advanced prostate cancer. PSA is a well-established screening test for prostate cancer and the oncologists wanted to examine the correlation between level of PSA and a number of clinical measures for men who were about to undergo radical prostatectomy. The measures are cancer volume, prostate weight, patient age, the amount of benign prostatic hyperplasia, seminal vesicle invasion, capsular penetration, and Gleason score. (50 pts)

Select a random sample of 65 observations to use as the train data set (Please use set.seed(567)) and reamining observations as the test data set.

Use the train data set to answer the following questions.

a-) Develop a best subset model for predicting PSA. Justify your choice of model. Assess your model’s ability to predict and discuss its usefulness to the oncologists.(5 pts)

text(tree_psa, pretty = 0)

# Assessing if  cross validation and pruning will improve the model

cv_tree_cancer  <- cv.tree(tree_psa, FUN = prune.tree)

names(cv_tree_cancer)
## [1] "size"   "dev"    "k"      "method"
cv_tree_cancer
## $size
## [1] 3 2 1
## 
## $dev
## [1]  69345.33  70231.14 112868.66
## 
## $k
## [1]      -Inf  2101.545 43318.697
## 
## $method
## [1] "deviance"
## 
## attr(,"class")
## [1] "prune"         "tree.sequence"
# checking the lowest deviance and the corresponding size to assess the best model.

# even though size = 3 has the lowest deviance , size= 2 has also similar deviance and also has less predictors. This would be a better and simpler tree.


pruned_tree_cancer <- prune.tree(tree_psa, best = 2)

plot(pruned_tree_cancer)
text(pruned_tree_cancer, pretty = 0)

summary(tree_psa)
## 
## Regression tree:
## tree(formula = PSA.level ~ ., data = cancer.train)
## Variables actually used in tree construction:
## [1] "Cancer.volume"
## Number of terminal nodes:  3 
## Residual mean deviance:  924.3 = 57310 / 62 
## Distribution of residuals:
##    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
## -76.570  -6.071  -2.181   0.000   8.050 173.600
summary(pruned_tree_cancer)
## 
## Regression tree:
## snip.tree(tree = tree_psa, nodes = 2L)
## Variables actually used in tree construction:
## [1] "Cancer.volume"
## Number of terminal nodes:  2 
## Residual mean deviance:  943 = 59410 / 63 
## Distribution of residuals:
##    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
## -76.570  -8.605  -2.894   0.000   4.946 173.600

CONCLUSION: The original tree has 3 terminal nodes. After doing cross validation , the tree size with The deviance is lowest when size of the tree is 3 which is the same node size of the original tree without pruning.

However, size = 2 also has similar and close deviance and would make more sense because only one variable- Cancer.volume has been used in the model without using any other predictors and also using 2 nodes is a simpler model than a 3 node tree . It also has a similar residual mean deviance of 943 which is also closer to the node 3 tree with 924 residual deviance.

Hence the tree with size = 2 is a better tree.

Interpretation of the regression tree :

1.Nodes -2 2. most important predictor –> Cancer.volume 3.Residual mean deviance: 943 = 59410 / 63

This is a simple tree with one split into 2 nodes with cancer volume the important predictor

c-) Develop a lasso regression model to predict PSA and interpret your model. (10 pts)

Step 1: find the best lambda

Step 2: use the best lambda to find the lasso model

Step3: Analyse the model

# loading the pkgs

install.packages("glmnet")
## Warning: package 'glmnet' is in use and will not be installed
library(glmnet)

#need to define X and Y matrix for glmnet

x <- model.matrix(PSA.level ~ ., data = cancer.train)[, -c(1)]  # Remove the intercept
y <- cancer.train$PSA.level

LassoMod <- glmnet(x, y, alpha=1, nlambda=100,lambda.min.ratio=0.0001)
plot(LassoMod,xvar="norm",label=TRUE)

CvLassoMod <- cv.glmnet(x, y, alpha=1, nlambda=100,lambda.min.ratio=0.0001)
plot(CvLassoMod)

best.lambda.lasso <- CvLassoMod$lambda.min
best.lambda.lasso
## [1] 1.779019
coef(CvLassoMod, s = "lambda.min")

The tree model can be easily explained that if the cancer volume is above 16, then Psa.level increases and if it is less than 16 , it decreases. On the other hand, the other models like the subset which has 4 predictors - Cancer.volume ,Weight, Age ,Capsular.penetration and would have to be explained on the changes of all these 4 variables and their corresponding coefficients. The lasso model also has 5 predictor variables and would also be difficult to explain in terms of these 5 variables and the changes cause in the PSA.level due to them ( according to the corr coefficients)

Overall, the tree model is the better model to explain in terms of ease of interpretation.
